faqs.q: Your interest is on land tied to the Ute Indian Tribe reservation. Can you still buy it?
faqs.a: In many cases yes, but the transfer process involves federal review that a purely private mineral sale doesn't. We'll explain the specific steps and timeline once we know the details of your interest.

faqs.q: Do you need a recent royalty statement to get started?
faqs.a: No. If you don't have one, we can research your interest through Utah's oil and gas records and the county recorder's office using your name or the property's legal description.

faqs.q: What if you want to think it over before accepting an offer?
faqs.a: That's completely fine. We don't put deadlines on our offers, and you're welcome to take as much time as you need to decide.

faqs.q: Is your interest state trust land instead of federal or private?
faqs.a: It's possible. Utah's School and Institutional Trust Lands Administration manages a significant amount of state trust minerals in the Uinta basin, and a transfer of those follows its own separate process from either private or federal minerals. We'll identify which category applies to you early on.

faqs.q: Does the type of crude affect how quickly you should decide whether to sell?
faqs.a: Uinta basin waxy crude has seen real swings tied to rail and pipeline capacity for moving it out of the basin, so market conditions can shift the picture over time. We're happy to revisit an offer if you'd rather wait and see how things develop before deciding.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Alabama
items.meta: Own Alabama mineral or royalty interests in the Black Warrior basin? We buy coalbed methane, conventional, and coal royalty from Alabama families. Free offer.

sections.html:
If your family's Alabama royalty check traces back to the Black Warrior basin, you're holding a piece of one of the oldest coalbed methane plays in the country.

We bought out our own coalbed methane interest in Tuscaloosa County years ago, so we know what it's like to hold a royalty statement from a well you've never seen and wonder if the number on it still means anything. Alabama mineral owners are a different breed than the ones you read about in Texas headlines — this state's production has always run quieter, built on coal seam gas instead of a shale boom, and a lot of the interests we see trace back to land grants, coal leases, or family splits that go back three or four generations.

Royalty Buyer USA buys mineral and royalty interests across Alabama, beyond only the coalbed methane acreage around Tuscaloosa, Fayette, and Walker counties. We also buy conventional oil and gas royalty from the smaller fields scattered through the southwest part of the state, and coal royalty where that's what your family actually holds. If you're not sure which kind of interest is on your deed, that's normal — we'll help you sort it out before we ever talk numbers.

sections.title: The Black Warrior basin and what makes it different
sections.html:
The Black Warrior basin was one of the first places coalbed methane got produced at commercial scale, starting back in the late 1970s and early 1980s. That means a lot of the wells tied to Alabama royalty interests are old by industry standards, and their production has been declining slowly and steadily for decades rather than falling off a cliff like a shale well does in its first two years. If your check has been shrinking a little every year for as long as you can remember, that's the basin doing exactly what a mature coalbed methane field does.

Because the play is mature, operators here don't drill much new acreage anymore. What that means for you as an owner is that the value of your interest is tied almost entirely to what's already producing and how many years of life the field has left — not to speculation about a future drilling program. We look at decline curves on Black Warrior wells every week, so when we make an offer on Tuscaloosa or Walker County acreage we're pricing it against real production history, not a guess.

sections.title: Coal, coalbed methane, and conventional — knowing which one you own
sections.html:
Alabama is one of the few states where a family can genuinely hold three different kinds of mineral interest under the same tract: the coal itself, the coalbed methane gas trapped in that same coal seam, and in some counties a shallow conventional oil or gas zone underneath it all. Old deeds sometimes severed these from each other, so your grandfather's 'mineral rights' might legally mean coal only, or coal and gas together, depending on how the severance was worded decades ago.

We read the deed language before we make an offer, because it changes what we're actually buying. If your interest includes coal royalty from an active or historical mine, we treat that as its own asset with its own value, separate from any gas royalty on the same tract. Owners who've never had this explained to them are often surprised to learn they're sitting on two or three distinct interests instead of one.

sections.title: Why Alabama royalty statements confuse so many owners
sections.html:
Coalbed methane royalty statements tend to carry more deductions than a lot of owners expect — gathering, compression, and dehydration charges are common on gas that has to be processed to pipeline quality straight out of the coal seam. That's not a red flag on its own; it's how the play has always worked. But it does mean two owners with the same percentage interest can see different net numbers depending on which gathering system their well ties into.

We've sat across the kitchen table from enough Alabama families to know the question that always comes up: is this check ever going to get bigger again. For most legacy Black Warrior interests, the honest answer is no — production declines, prices move, and the number on the statement is more likely to drift down over the coming years than up. That's part of why some owners choose to sell now, converting decades of future small checks into one payment they can use today.

sections.title: How a sale works if you decide to move forward
sections.html:
We start with your county, your legal description if you have it, and copies of a few recent statements. From there we pull production and pricing history on the specific wells or leases tied to your interest and build an offer that reflects what that acreage has actually produced, hedged against how coalbed methane in this basin typically performs as it matures. We're not appraisers or attorneys, and for anything involving your estate, taxes, or a title dispute, talk to your own CPA or attorney — we'll never tell you otherwise.

Once you accept, we handle the title work, draft the assignment, and close through a title company or attorney's escrow, the same way any real estate closing in Alabama would run. Most owners are paid within a few weeks of sending back a signed offer, and there's no cost to you to get a number and decide whether it makes sense.

faqs.q: Do you buy coal royalty in Alabama, or only oil and gas?
faqs.a: Both. We buy coal royalty, coalbed methane royalty, and conventional oil and gas royalty across Alabama, including tracts where a family holds more than one kind under the same deed.

faqs.q: Your coalbed methane well in Tuscaloosa County has been producing since the 1980s. Is it worth anything now?
faqs.a: Often yes, though the value reflects a mature, declining asset rather than a growth play. We price offers against the actual decline curve of your specific well, so an older well isn't automatically worth less per acre than a younger one — it depends on remaining reserves and current pricing.

faqs.q: Your deed only mentions 'minerals' with no split between coal and gas. How do you handle that?
faqs.a: We read the full chain of title, beyond only your current deed, because older severances upstream can determine what 'minerals' actually covers on your tract. We'll explain what we find before making an offer, and recommend you have your own attorney review anything you're uncertain about.

faqs.q: Why does your Alabama royalty check have so many deductions on it?
faqs.a: Coalbed methane gas typically requires gathering, compression, and dehydration to reach pipeline quality, and those costs are commonly passed through to royalty owners under standard Alabama lease terms. It's normal for this play, though the exact deductions vary by which gathering system your well uses.

faqs.q: Do you have to sell your whole interest, or can you sell part of it?
faqs.a: We can typically buy a partial interest, a specific well, or your entire mineral position, depending on what makes sense for your family. Tell us what you're comfortable parting with and we'll structure the offer around that.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Mississippi
items.meta: TMS or Jurassic salt basin royalty in Mississippi runs through the county courthouse first. We handle that legwork and buy your interest. Free offer.

sections.html:
Before we ever quote a Mississippi mineral interest, somebody on our end has usually already spent time at the county chancery clerk's office confirming what the record actually shows.

Mississippi mineral title runs through the chancery clerk in each county, not a centralized state registry, which means confirming ownership on an older Mississippi tract is genuinely courthouse work, pulling deed books, checking indexes, and sometimes finding that the last recorded transfer was two generations ago and nobody since has bothered to record the family's changes in ownership. We've done that legwork in a lot of Mississippi counties by now, from the Tuscaloosa Marine Shale counties along the southwestern border to the older Jurassic salt basin fields further east.

The state's two big plays sit in different parts of Mississippi and carry different histories. The Tuscaloosa Marine Shale runs through counties like Amite, Wilkinson, and Franklin along the Louisiana border, an oil play that's had real leasing interest but uneven drilling results over the years. The Jurassic salt basin fields, including legacy production tied to salt dome structures across the central and southern part of the state, have been producing in some cases since the mid-1900s, with ownership records that go back just as far.

sections.title: Why the courthouse comes first in Mississippi
sections.html:
Because chancery clerk records are county-specific and not always fully indexed online, especially for older deeds, we don't take a Mississippi owner's word for their percentage interest at face value, not out of distrust, but because it's common for the record to show something slightly different from what a family remembers, especially after multiple inheritances. A deed recorded in 1962 might have language that changes how a 2026 heir's share actually calculates out.

We pull that record ourselves before making an offer, and we explain what we find in plain terms. If your interest turns out to be different from what you expected, we'd rather tell you honestly upfront than build an offer around a number that won't hold up at closing.

sections.title: Tuscaloosa Marine Shale: leased hard, drilled unevenly
sections.html:
TMS acreage in southwest Mississippi has gone through cycles where operators leased aggressively expecting strong results, followed by quieter periods when drilling slowed after wells underperformed early expectations elsewhere in the play. If your family's acreage is in an active TMS area right now, that's meaningfully different from acreage that was leased years ago and has seen no drilling since.

We check current, specific activity near your tract rather than pricing based on the play's broader reputation, and we're candid when a TMS interest looks like speculative upside rather than a proven, producing asset.

sections.title: Jurassic salt basin legacy production
sections.html:
Mississippi's salt dome-associated fields, tied to the deep Jurassic Smackover and related formations, have produced oil and gas for the better part of a century in parts of the state, and ownership on some of these tracts is now several generations removed from whoever originally signed the lease. These are often smaller, steady-decline interests rather than active new plays, similar in character to legacy production we see in Alabama and Louisiana.

We price these against long, well-documented production histories where they exist, and we're upfront if a well appears to be nearing the end of its economic life rather than inflating expectations.

sections.title: Selling once title is confirmed
sections.html:
Once we've confirmed your interest through the chancery clerk records, the offer and closing process runs like it does in any other state: a written offer explaining our reasoning, closing through a title company or attorney's escrow, and payment typically within a few weeks of your acceptance. If the courthouse research turns up a title issue, like an unrecorded transfer or unfinished probate, we'll tell you what needs to happen before a clean sale can close.

There's no cost to start this process, and no obligation to move forward once you see the number.

faqs.q: Why does confirming your Mississippi mineral interest take longer than in some other states?
faqs.a: Mississippi title work runs through each county's chancery clerk rather than a centralized registry, and older deeds aren't always fully indexed online, so confirming ownership sometimes requires direct courthouse research.

faqs.q: What if the courthouse records don't match what your family always understood we owned?
faqs.a: It happens more often than you'd think, especially after multiple inheritances. We'll explain exactly what the record shows and how that affects your actual share before making an offer.

faqs.q: Is TMS acreage in Mississippi a sure thing?
faqs.a: No, the play has had uneven results and periods of slower activity since it was first leased. We evaluate current, real activity near your specific tract rather than the play's overall reputation.

faqs.q: Your family's salt basin interest has been producing since the 1950s. Is it near the end of its life?
faqs.a: Possibly, and we'll tell you honestly based on the well's actual decline data rather than assuming either way. Many of these legacy Mississippi wells are in the later stages of a long, slow decline.

faqs.q: What happens if there's a title problem, like an unrecorded transfer?
faqs.a: We'll explain what we found and what would need to happen, often a recorded affidavit or a probate, before a sale can close cleanly. We recommend a Mississippi attorney for that piece of the work.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Kentucky
items.meta: Coal, oil, and gas mineral rights in Kentucky can be owned separately under the same land. We help you sort it out and buy your royalty. Free offer.

sections.html:
In Kentucky, more than in most states, 'mineral rights' can legally mean three completely different things depending on which one your family's deed actually severed.

Ask ten Kentucky mineral owners what they own and you'll often get an answer like 'the minerals,' as if that settles it. It rarely does. Eastern Kentucky's Appalachian edge counties have a long history of coal mining, and old deeds from the early and mid-1900s frequently severed coal from oil and gas, sometimes even severing the right to mine the coal from ownership of the coal itself. Western Kentucky, sitting on the edge of the Illinois basin, has a different history built more around conventional oil and gas production with fewer coal complications.

We buy oil and gas royalty, mineral interests, and where it applies, coal royalty across Kentucky, but the first real work on any Kentucky page or any Kentucky phone call is figuring out which of those you're actually holding, because the deed language genuinely varies tract by tract in ways that surprise a lot of owners.

sections.title: Why coal and oil/gas got split apart in the first place
sections.html:
Through much of the 20th century, coal companies in eastern Kentucky bought or leased the coal seams under huge amounts of land, often leaving the surface owner with everything else, or sometimes leaving oil and gas rights with a separate party entirely. Layer decades of resales, inheritances, and company mergers on top of that, and you get tracts where the coal is owned by one entity, the oil and gas by another, and the surface by a third family who may have no mineral rights at all.

This means two neighbors on the same road can have completely different answers to 'do you own your minerals,' and it means we can't assume anything about your Kentucky interest until we've actually read the severance language in your chain of title.

sections.title: Reading your deed before we talk numbers
sections.html:
Before we make any offer on a Kentucky interest, we pull the deed history and confirm exactly what was severed, what you inherited, and whether coal, oil and gas, or both are included. If your grandfather's deed says 'coal and mining rights' with no mention of oil and gas, that's a meaningfully different asset than a deed that says 'all minerals,' even though both might get called 'mineral rights' around the kitchen table.

We explain what we find in plain language, not legal jargon, and if anything looks genuinely ambiguous, we'll say so and suggest you get your own attorney's read before moving forward. Better to know now than after a closing.

sections.title: Appalachian edge coal royalty and what drives its value
sections.html:
Coal royalty in Kentucky's Appalachian counties depends heavily on which seam is involved, whether it's currently being actively mined or sits idle, and how national coal demand and pricing have shifted, which has been a difficult trend for coal broadly over the past decade. We're honest about that headwind rather than pretending coal royalty carries the same outlook it did fifty years ago.

Where coal royalty is still active and producing, we value it on real production and pricing data specific to that mine and seam, the same disciplined approach we use for oil and gas.

sections.title: Illinois basin oil and gas in western Kentucky
sections.html:
Western Kentucky counties along the Illinois basin's southern edge have a longer, quieter oil and gas history, with a lot of shallow conventional wells that have produced steadily for decades without the coal severance complications common in the eastern part of the state. If your interest sits in this region, valuing it looks more like our approach in Illinois — decline curve and remaining reserve life on wells that have often been producing a long time.

Wherever in Kentucky your interest sits, we start the same way: confirm the deed, confirm the production, and build an honest offer from there. There's no cost to get a number, and no pressure to accept it.

faqs.q: Your deed only mentions coal. Does that mean you do not own oil and gas rights too?
faqs.a: It might, or it might not — it depends entirely on the exact severance language in your specific chain of title. We read the full history before assuming anything either way.

faqs.q: Do you buy coal royalty, or just oil and gas?
faqs.a: We buy both where they apply, along with combined mineral interests, but we treat coal and oil/gas as separate assets since Kentucky deeds frequently severed them from each other.

faqs.q: Is coal royalty worth less than it used to be?
faqs.a: In many cases yes, reflecting the broader decline in national coal demand over the past decade. We price coal royalty on real, current production and pricing rather than historical highs.

faqs.q: Your family's interest is in western Kentucky, not the coal counties. Is that different?
faqs.a: Yes, western Kentucky's Illinois basin edge tends to be conventional oil and gas without the coal-severance complications common in eastern Kentucky, so the ownership picture is often more straightforward.

faqs.q: How do you find out what your deed actually severed?
faqs.a: Send us what you have, even if it's incomplete, and we'll research the chain of title and explain what we find in plain language before making an offer.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Tennessee
items.meta: Small, quiet mineral interest in eastern Tennessee? We buy modest Appalachian-edge royalty and mineral shares other buyers often skip past.

sections.html:
Most companies buying minerals want big, active tracts in busy plays, which leaves a lot of quiet Tennessee owners with a small interest and nobody willing to make a real offer.

We know what it's like to hold something that everyone else treats as too small to bother with. Tennessee sits on the edge of Appalachian oil and gas country, mostly in the eastern counties, and its production has always been modest compared to neighbors like Kentucky, Virginia, and West Virginia. That doesn't mean your interest has no value, it just means most of the big national buyers never bother looking closely at it.

We do. If you have a small royalty check coming from an old well in Scott, Fentress, Overton, or one of the other eastern counties, or a mineral interest with no active production at all, we'll take a real look and give you a straightforward answer instead of a form letter.

sections.title: A modest but real oil and gas history
sections.html:
Tennessee's oil and gas production has never rivaled its Appalachian neighbors, but the eastern part of the state has a genuine, decades-long history of shallow conventional wells, particularly in the Cumberland Plateau counties. Production per well tends to be small, and much of it has been in slow decline for years, which is exactly the kind of interest that big buyers skip past because the dollar amounts don't move their needle. That's a mismatch of scale, not a sign your interest is worthless.

We're set up to evaluate these smaller interests properly, checking your actual statements or, if you're not currently receiving any, the county's oil and gas records to understand what's historically been produced nearby.

sections.title: What a small, steady well is actually worth
sections.html: A shallow conventional well with a long, slow decline is a different animal than a modern shale well, but it's not automatically less valuable per dollar of monthly income. These older wells often decline gradually rather than steeply, which means the income, while modest, can be more predictable than people assume. We look at your actual check history over time to understand that pattern before putting a number together, rather than assuming a small check means a small opportunity.

sections.title: Interests with no current production
sections.html: A fair number of Tennessee mineral owners hold interests that aren't producing at all right now, sometimes because a well was plugged years ago, sometimes because the acreage was never drilled. We're honest that non-producing interests in Tennessee carry lower near-term value than a producing well, given how limited current drilling activity is statewide, but we still make offers on them, particularly when there's a documented production history nearby that suggests real potential.

sections.title: Family land in the Cumberland Plateau
sections.html: A lot of the mineral ownership we see in eastern Tennessee is tied to family farms and timberland that have been passed down for generations, often with the mineral rights split among more relatives than anyone's kept straight track of. If you're managing an estate that includes one of these interests, we can look at just your piece of it, explain what it's worth in plain terms, and let you decide without pressure.

faqs.q: Is your Tennessee mineral interest too small for you to buy?
faqs.a: No. We regularly buy modest interests that larger national buyers pass on, including small shares from shallow conventional wells or non-producing acreage.

faqs.q: Your well only pays a small amount each month. Is it still worth selling?
faqs.a: It can be. Small, steady wells often have a long, predictable decline, and we price that predictability rather than dismissing an interest just because the monthly amount is modest.

faqs.q: Your interest doesn't have an active well right now. Will you still make an offer?
faqs.a: Yes, though non-producing acreage in Tennessee typically prices lower given limited current drilling activity statewide. We'll still look at the historical production nearby before deciding on a fair number.

faqs.q: How do you find out about production if you do not have recent statements?
faqs.a: We check Tennessee's oil and gas records and the relevant county's recorded documents directly, so you don't need to track down old paperwork yourself.

faqs.q: Your family's mineral rights are split among a lot of relatives. Can you buy just your share?
faqs.a: Yes, we can make an offer on your specific fractional share without requiring every family member to participate.

faqs.q: Which Tennessee counties actually have oil and gas production?
faqs.a: Most of the state's activity sits in the eastern Cumberland Plateau counties, including Scott, Fentress, Overton, Morgan, and Pickett, where shallow conventional wells have operated for decades. Activity elsewhere in the state is much rarer.

faqs.q: How do you value an interest if your well was plugged years ago?
faqs.a: We look at the well's production history while it was active, along with any activity on nearby tracts, to understand what the acreage has demonstrated it can produce, even though the specific well is no longer operating.

faqs.q: Is it worth getting your Tennessee mineral rights appraised before selling?
faqs.a: For a modest interest, a formal appraisal often costs more than it's worth. We're glad to explain our reasoning in detail so you can judge the offer for yourself without needing to pay for outside review.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Nebraska
items.meta: Own minerals in Nebraska's panhandle or DJ basin edge counties? Get a straightforward cash offer from a family that's been on your side of the closing table.

sections.html:
If you own minerals in Nebraska, chances are you've spent more time explaining what you have to people than actually getting an answer about what it's worth.

We're a family that sold our own minerals years back, and one thing we learned quickly is that owning minerals in a state most people don't associate with oil and gas makes everything harder. Nebraska doesn't come up in the same conversations as Texas or North Dakota, but the panhandle counties along the Colorado and Wyoming lines sit right on the edge of the Denver-Julesburg basin and the Niobrara formation, and interests there have real value even if activity has been quiet for a stretch.

Whether your minerals came from a family homestead, an inheritance nobody's fully sorted out, or a lease your parents signed decades ago that's sat dormant since, we'll take a real look at it. You won't get a form letter with a lowball number attached. You'll get someone who actually looked at your county.

sections.title: Nebraska's place on the map
sections.html:
Banner, Kimball, and Cheyenne counties sit on the eastern edge of the DJ basin, which stretches across into Colorado and Wyoming where most of the Niobrara drilling has historically happened. Nebraska's side of that edge has seen far less activity, and what has happened tends to run in short bursts tied to commodity prices rather than a steady development program. That makes valuing an interest here less about pointing to a nearby well and more about understanding regional trends and what operators have actually filed for in the area.

Because the state doesn't see much drilling news, a lot of owners assume their minerals are essentially worthless. That's not always true. Undeveloped minerals in a play's flank counties still carry option value, since operators periodically test the edges of a basin when core acreage gets crowded, and pricing should reflect that possibility rather than assume it's zero.

sections.title: How we price a quiet county
sections.html:
When there's little or no recent activity, we look at what's happening just across the state line, how operators have historically treated the edge of the Niobrara play, and any permit or lease activity on record for your specific township. We're honest that a non-producing tract in a quiet county will price lower than a producing interest in an active basin, but we don't price it at zero just because there's no well nearby right now.

If you do have a producing interest, even an older well with modest volumes, that changes the conversation. A real production history, however small, gives us something concrete to work from instead of general regional trends.

sections.title: Family land, split ownership
sections.html:
A lot of the mineral ownership we see in Nebraska traces back to homestead-era land patents, where the family kept the minerals when the surface was sold, or split evenly among children generations ago. That means many owners today hold a small fractional share, sometimes an eighth or a sixteenth, in a section they've never seen. Tracking down the rest of the family, agreeing on what to do, and getting everyone's paperwork together is often more work than the interest itself feels worth.

We can buy your specific fractional share directly without needing every co-owner to participate. If your siblings or cousins want to sell too, we're glad to make offers on their shares as well, but it's never a requirement.

sections.title: What to expect if you reach out
sections.html: We start by asking a few questions about the county, the legal description if you have it, and whether the interest is producing or not. From there we check the county records ourselves rather than asking you to dig up paperwork you may not have. You'll get a plain offer with the reasoning behind it, and you can take as long as you need to decide.

faqs.q: Is your Nebraska mineral interest worth anything if there's no well nearby?
faqs.a: It can be, depending on how close you are to active DJ basin or Niobrara acreage and what operators have leased or permitted recently in your area. We look at regional trends rather than assuming no nearby well means no value.

faqs.q: If you only own a small fractional interest inherited from a homestead. Can you still buy it?
faqs.a: Yes, we regularly buy fractional interests like these, and you don't need the rest of your family to sell alongside you.

faqs.q: How do you find out about your county if there's not much public information?
faqs.a: We pull county records directly, check surrounding lease and permit activity, and look at how the basin has developed across the state line, rather than relying only on what's publicly discussed about Nebraska specifically.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer to sell your minerals?
faqs.a: It's not required, though for larger or more complicated interests, some owners like to have their attorney review the deed before signing. We're happy to work alongside your advisor if you have one.

faqs.q: How long does closing usually take?
faqs.a: Once title is confirmed at the county courthouse, most Nebraska closings move quickly, often within a couple of weeks, though older or more complex title can take longer.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Michigan
items.meta: Antrim shale royalty check gotten smaller every year? That's normal for Michigan's legacy gas play. We buy Michigan mineral interests. Free offer.

sections.html:
If you've held an Antrim shale royalty interest since the 1990s and watched the check get a little smaller almost every year since, you're not imagining it, and you're not doing anything wrong.

There's a particular kind of tired that comes from watching something shrink slowly over twenty or thirty years and wondering if you should have done something about it sooner. We hear that from Michigan owners more than almost anywhere else, because the Antrim shale, drilled heavily across the northern Lower Peninsula through the 1980s and 90s, is one of the oldest continuously producing shale gas plays in the country, and it has been quietly declining for a very long time.

We buy Antrim shale royalty and other Michigan oil and gas interests, and we specialize in exactly this kind of legacy position: an interest that's been paying steadily smaller amounts for years, where the owner isn't sure if it's still worth anything or if it's finally time to turn the last of it into one payment instead of another decade of shrinking checks.

sections.title: Why the Antrim shale behaves the way it does
sections.html:
Antrim shale wells produce gas along with a significant amount of water, and their production profile is different from a modern horizontal shale well — they tend to build slowly to a peak over the first few years, then decline gradually and predictably for a long stretch afterward, sometimes staying in production for well over two decades. If your check has followed a long, slow downward slope rather than a sharp drop, that's the Antrim doing exactly what Antrim wells do.

Because so many Antrim wells have now been producing for twenty-plus years, most of the play is deep into that long tail of decline. New drilling in the Antrim is rare today, so like a lot of the mature plays we work in, value here comes almost entirely from what's left in the ground and how many more years the well realistically has, not from any prospect of new activity.

sections.title: Reading a Michigan royalty statement that's been shrinking for years
sections.html:
A statement that's a fraction of what it was ten years ago isn't a sign your interest has gone bad, it's the natural arc of a mature gas well nearing the end of its economic life. The honest question worth asking isn't whether the check will bounce back, for most legacy Antrim interests it won't, but how many more years of a shrinking check you're likely looking at, and whether that total is worth more to you as one payment now.

We build our offers around exactly that math: what your well has left, discounted for the fact that gas wells this mature typically decline further before they stop, priced against current natural gas pricing rather than what gas was worth when your interest was first leased decades ago.

sections.title: Ownership that's often changed hands more than the well has
sections.html:
A lot of Antrim interests have been inherited once or twice by now, since the play is old enough that original lessors have often passed the interest down to children or grandchildren. If you inherited your interest and never got a full explanation of what it is or where it comes from, that's common, and we're happy to walk through what we find in the record with you before you decide anything.

We also see interests that were split among siblings at inheritance, so if you only hold a fraction of what your parents originally owned, that's still something we can quote and buy on its own.

sections.title: What a Michigan sale looks like from here
sections.html:
Send us your county, the well or lease name if you have it, and a recent statement, and we'll pull the production history ourselves. Northern Lower Peninsula counties like Otsego, Antrim, and Kalkaska have decades of Antrim data available, which lets us build a confident decline projection rather than a rough guess.

Once you accept an offer, we handle the paperwork and close through a title company or attorney escrow, typically within a few weeks. There's no cost to find out what a mature Michigan interest like this is actually worth today.

faqs.q: Your Antrim shale check has gotten smaller every year for over a decade. Is that normal?
faqs.a: Yes, this is the typical long, slow decline pattern for Antrim shale wells, which is different from the sharper early decline of a modern horizontal well. It doesn't mean anything is wrong with your interest.

faqs.q: Will your Antrim royalty ever go back up?
faqs.a: For most legacy Antrim interests, no, since new drilling in the play is rare today and the wells are deep into their natural decline. Occasional upticks from gas pricing are possible, but the long-term trend is downward.

faqs.q: You inherited a small piece of a larger family interest. Can you still buy just your share?
faqs.a: Yes, we regularly buy individual heirs' fractional shares of a larger family interest, even when it's been split among several siblings.

faqs.q: How do you value a well that's been declining for over 20 years?
faqs.a: We build a decline projection from the well's long production history, which for mature Antrim wells is usually well documented, and price the remaining years against current natural gas pricing.

faqs.q: Is it better to keep collecting a small check or sell now?
faqs.a: That depends on your personal situation and how many more years of production your specific well likely has left. We'll walk through the math honestly so you can decide for yourself.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Illinois
items.meta: Own stripper well or legacy Illinois basin royalty passed down for generations? We buy small Illinois oil and gas interests other buyers skip. Free offer.

sections.html:
Illinois basin oil has been quietly producing since before either of your grandparents were born, off wells most people driving past would never notice.

Our own family sold a small stripper-well interest years back, a handful of dollars a month that had been in the family so long nobody remembered exactly when it started, and we know how easy it is to assume a check that small isn't worth anyone's time to buy. Illinois is full of interests like that. The Illinois basin, stretching across the southern third of the state through counties like Marion, Clay, Wayne, and Fayette, has been producing oil since the early 1900s, and a huge share of that production today comes from stripper wells — low-volume wells that keep pumping a few barrels a day, sometimes for a hundred years.

We buy these interests specifically, including the small ones a lot of buyers skip because the math doesn't excite them the way a Permian deal does. If your family holds a fractional interest tied to a well that's been producing since your great-grandparents' time, or a royalty that's shrunk to a few dollars a quarter, we still want to look at it.

sections.title: What a hundred-year-old stripper well actually means for value
sections.html:
A well that's been producing for a century isn't unusual in the Illinois basin — it's close to normal. These wells decline extremely slowly once they reach a certain low, stable production level, sometimes holding at a nearly flat rate for decades at a time rather than falling off the way a modern shale well does in its first few years. That stability is actually a useful thing to know when we value your interest, because it means we can project remaining life with more confidence than we could on a newer, steeper-declining well.

The tradeoff is volume: these wells were never big producers, and they're not going to become big producers now. Value on Illinois basin stripper interests tends to come from consistency and remaining years of production rather than size, and we price accordingly, using real per-well data from the specific lease your interest sits on.

sections.title: Small interests, real ownership
sections.html:
A lot of Illinois mineral interests have been divided across generations of heirs, so it's common for someone to own a fraction of a fraction, a decimal interest with a lot of zeros after the decimal point. That doesn't mean the interest isn't real or isn't worth pursuing; it just means the total dollar value is smaller and the paperwork sometimes takes a bit more digging to confirm.

We work with owners on interests this small regularly, and we don't treat them as too minor to bother with. If you have even a partial statement or an old division order with your name on it, that's usually enough for us to start tracking down the rest.

sections.title: Illinois basin counties we see the most activity in
sections.html:
Marion, Clay, Wayne, Fayette, and Jefferson counties account for a large share of the state's ongoing production, along with pockets further south and west. Most of this activity is conventional oil from shallow formations, not the horizontal shale drilling you'd see in Colorado or North Dakota, which is part of why the wells behave so differently and why Illinois rarely makes national oil and gas headlines despite over a century of continuous production.

Wherever your interest sits within the basin, we research the specific lease and well history in that county rather than applying a blanket statewide number, because production and remaining life vary meaningfully even between neighboring counties.

sections.title: Selling a small Illinois interest without the runaround
sections.html:
Because these interests are often modest in size, we try to keep the process proportionate — we don't need a mountain of paperwork to get started, just your county, the well or lease name if you have it, and a recent statement or division order. From there we confirm production, build an offer, and explain how we arrived at it.

If your interest turns out to be tied up in an incomplete estate or unclear title, which happens often with older Illinois interests split across many heirs, we'll tell you honestly and point you toward an attorney for that piece. Otherwise, most sales close within a few weeks through a title company or attorney's escrow, with no cost to you to get a number.

faqs.q: Your Illinois royalty check is only a few dollars a quarter. Is it even worth selling?
faqs.a: It can be, since even small stripper well interests carry a value based on remaining production life. We'll give you an honest number so you can decide if it's worth the effort for your situation.

faqs.q: How can a well still be producing after 100 years?
faqs.a: Many Illinois basin wells reach a low, stable production rate and hold there for decades with very slow decline, which is common for this basin's shallow conventional formations and different from how a modern shale well behaves.

faqs.q: If you only own a tiny fractional interest split among a lot of cousins. Do you still buy those?
faqs.a: Yes, we regularly buy small fractional interests, even when a tract has been divided many times across generations of heirs.

faqs.q: You do not have much paperwork, just an old check stub. Can you still help?
faqs.a: Usually yes. A check stub, division order, or old statement is often enough for us to start researching the well and lease behind it.

faqs.q: Do you buy interests in every Illinois basin county, or just the biggest ones?
faqs.a: We buy across the basin, including smaller counties with modest production, beyond only Marion or Wayne County. Send us your county and we'll look into it.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Missouri
items.meta: Small Forest City basin royalty in Missouri that most buyers ignore? We buy modest, non-operated Missouri mineral interests other companies pass on.

sections.html:
Missouri isn't a state most royalty buyers advertise for, and honestly, that's exactly why the owners who do call us are often glad they found somebody willing to look.

We grew up around ranch land, not oil fields, and the first mineral interest we ever sold ourselves was small and unglamorous, tucked on the margin of a basin nobody talked about much. That's basically the story of Missouri mineral ownership. The Forest City basin, which extends across northwest Missouri along the edge of a larger multi-state basin centered further north and west, has never been a major national oil and gas story, and production here has always run modest by comparison to Kansas or Oklahoma next door.

That doesn't mean Missouri interests aren't real or aren't worth pursuing. We buy modest, non-operated royalty and mineral interests across the Missouri portion of the Forest City basin, the kind of small, quiet position a lot of larger buyers skip because the numbers don't move the needle on their end. They can still matter on yours, and we treat them that way.

sections.title: Why Missouri gets overlooked by most mineral buyers
sections.html:
The Forest City basin has produced conventional oil and gas for decades, mostly from shallow, low-volume wells rather than anything resembling a modern shale play, and total statewide production has always been small compared to neighboring Kansas. Because of that, a lot of national mineral-buying companies simply don't build out Missouri-specific research, and some won't even quote an interest here at all.

We don't skip it. Small and steady is still a real category of value, and we're set up to research individual wells and leases in Missouri counties the same way we do in bigger, more famous basins, even when the dollar amounts involved are modest.

sections.title: What ownership typically looks like on the basin's edge
sections.html:
Being on the edge of a basin rather than its productive core usually means thinner pay zones, lower per-well volumes, and interests that were often leased decades ago and have quietly kept producing at a low, stable rate ever since. A lot of Missouri owners we talk to inherited an interest from a family member who farmed the surface and happened to also own the minerals, a more common pairing here than in states where minerals were severed early and often.

Because these are usually smaller interests, ownership tends to be less fractured across many heirs than what we see in some other legacy states, though it's not unheard of. Either way, we start by confirming exactly what you hold before discussing value.

sections.title: Valuing a modest, non-operated interest honestly
sections.html:
A small check doesn't mean a worthless interest, but it does mean the value conversation looks different than it would for an active shale unit. We look at how long the well has been producing, how stable that production has been, and what realistic remaining life looks like, then price the interest against that, using hedged ranges tied to current activity rather than a flat promise.

We also tell Missouri owners plainly when an interest looks genuinely marginal, close to the end of its economic life, because that's useful information even if you decide to keep it rather than sell.

sections.title: Selling a Missouri interest without the runaround
sections.html:
Send us your county, any lease or well information you have, and a recent statement if you have one. If you don't have much documentation, that's alright too; small, older interests sometimes came with thin paperwork to begin with, and we can often track down more from county and state records.

If you decide to move forward, we handle title work and close through a title company or attorney escrow, typically within a few weeks. There's no cost to get a number, even for a small interest most other buyers wouldn't bother pricing.

faqs.q: Do you actually buy small Missouri mineral interests, or just big ones elsewhere?
faqs.a: We buy modest Forest City basin interests specifically, including small, non-operated positions that a lot of larger buyers skip because the dollar amounts are smaller than what they typically pursue.

faqs.q: Why don't more companies buy minerals in Missouri?
faqs.a: Missouri's Forest City basin has always produced modestly compared to neighboring states, so many national buyers haven't built out Missouri-specific research and simply don't quote interests here.

faqs.q: Your family owns both the surface and the minerals. Does that make selling the minerals different?
faqs.a: Not fundamentally, though it does mean the mineral interest hasn't been severed and traded separately for generations the way it has in some other states, which can make title confirmation more straightforward.

faqs.q: You barely have any paperwork on your Missouri interest. Can you still help?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Older, smaller Missouri interests often came with thin original paperwork, and we can research county and state production records to fill in the gaps.

faqs.q: What if your well is close to the end of its productive life?
faqs.a: We'll tell you that honestly based on the production data, since it's useful information whether you decide to sell now or continue holding the interest.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in California
items.meta: Own royalty from the San Joaquin or LA basin fields your family has held for generations? We buy California mineral and royalty interests. Free offer.

sections.html:
A lot of California mineral interests we see aren't new deals at all — they're royalty that's been quietly in the family since before the interstate highway system existed.

There's a particular kind of California royalty owner we talk to often: someone whose great-grandfather owned a ranch outside Bakersfield or a lot near Long Beach back when nobody thought twice about signing an oil lease, and whose family has been getting a check, sometimes tiny, sometimes not, ever since. Kern County's San Joaquin basin and the old LA basin fields around Long Beach, Signal Hill, and Huntington Beach are some of the longest continuously producing oil country in America, and the ownership on a lot of that acreage hasn't changed hands in generations.

That kind of longevity creates its own problems. Deeds get split among more heirs every generation, records from the 1920s and 1930s are harder to track down, and nobody currently holding the interest may have ever met the person who originally signed the lease. We buy California royalty and mineral interests in both the San Joaquin and LA basin legacy fields, and we're used to working through title histories that go back further than most other states we operate in.

sections.title: San Joaquin basin: still one of the most productive oil regions in the country
sections.html:
Kern County alone has produced more oil than most entire states, and fields like Kern River, Midway-Sunset, and Elk Hills have been in production for over a century using increasingly sophisticated techniques to keep pulling from reservoirs that would have been considered depleted decades ago. That long, steady production history actually helps us when we value your interest — we have enormous amounts of decline and pricing data to work from, more than almost anywhere else in the country.

Steam-flood and other enhanced recovery methods common in the San Joaquin basin change how a well declines compared to a conventional shale play, often flattening the curve out for years at a time. We factor that into any offer rather than applying a generic decline model that doesn't match how these older California fields actually behave.

sections.title: The LA basin's urban oil fields
sections.html:
Signal Hill, Huntington Beach, Long Beach, and parts of the LA basin still host active oil production tucked between neighborhoods, golf courses, and shopping centers, often disguised behind decorative screening so most people driving by never realize a working pumpjack is there. Royalty tied to these urban fields carries its own regulatory pressure, since California has tightened rules and, in some areas, moved toward phasing out new permitting near residential zones over the coming years.

That regulatory direction is worth being honest about: it can affect the long-term outlook for continued drilling on some LA basin acreage, even where existing wells keep producing under grandfathered permits. We factor known regulatory constraints into our offers rather than pricing your interest as if nothing has changed.

sections.title: Old deeds, split heirs, and unclear title
sections.html:
Because so much California mineral ownership traces back many decades, it's common for an interest to now be held by a dozen or more heirs, some of whom may not even know they own a piece of it. Probate that was never fully completed, name changes, and county records that predate digital indexing all add friction to confirming exactly who owns what percentage.

We work through that kind of title regularly, and we don't expect you to have it all sorted out before you call us. If your family's interest needs a probate or a quiet title action before it can transfer cleanly, we'll tell you that upfront, and recommend you use your own attorney for that piece of the work rather than trying to handle it ourselves.

sections.title: What selling looks like for a California legacy interest
sections.html:
We start with whatever documentation you have, even if it's a decades-old statement or a name on an inherited deed with no other paperwork attached. From there we research the well or unit, confirm current operator and production, and build an offer based on real decline history for that specific field, hedged against how mature California oil generally performs over time.

Because these are often multi-heir interests, we're used to coordinating a sale across several family members at once, each signing their own portion. There's no cost to get a number, and if your title needs cleanup first, we'll point you toward that step rather than pretending it isn't necessary.

faqs.q: Your family's California oil interest goes back to the 1930s. Is it too old to sell?
faqs.a: No. Age doesn't disqualify an interest, though older deeds sometimes need a title review to confirm the current chain of ownership before a sale can close cleanly.

faqs.q: Does California's regulatory environment affect what your royalty is worth?
faqs.a: It can, particularly for LA basin acreage near residential areas where new permitting has tightened. We account for known regulatory constraints honestly when we build an offer rather than ignoring them.

faqs.q: There are six of us who inherited shares of the same interest. Can you buy from all of us at once?
faqs.a: Yes, we regularly work with multiple heirs on the same interest, and each person can decide separately whether to sell their share.

faqs.q: Why does your San Joaquin basin well still produce after 80-plus years?
faqs.a: Many San Joaquin fields use steam-flood and other enhanced recovery methods that extend a reservoir's productive life far beyond what conventional drilling alone would achieve, which is why some of these wells have been active for generations.

faqs.q: What if your family's title isn't clean yet, like an unfinished probate?
faqs.a: We'll tell you honestly if that's the case and recommend you handle probate or title cleanup with your own attorney first. We can often still work with you on a timeline while that's underway.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Alaska
items.meta: Hold a North Slope royalty or overriding royalty interest in Alaska? We buy oil, gas, and non-op royalty from Alaska owners nationwide. No obligation offer.

sections.html:
North Slope royalty rarely looks like a Texas ranch royalty check — it's more often an ANCSA-linked interest, a working interest override, or a small legacy position that's been passed down without much explanation.

We come from ranching stock, not the oil patch, so when we started buying minerals we had to learn Alaska's ownership patterns from scratch — and they're genuinely unlike anywhere else in the country. Much of the North Slope sits on state and Native corporation land rather than the checkerboard of private mineral estates you'd find in Oklahoma or Texas, which means the royalty and overriding royalty interests that do exist in private hands often came from an early participation agreement, a farmout, or a family member who worked the industry decades ago and kept a piece.

If you're one of the relatively small number of people nationwide holding an Alaska oil and gas royalty or ORRI, whether it's tied to Prudhoe Bay, Kuparuk, or one of the newer discoveries on the Slope, we buy those interests. We also buy non-operated working interests and net profits interests where that's what someone actually holds. Because these positions are less common and less liquid than a typical Permian royalty, getting a real offer usually means more legwork on our end — legwork we do before we ever quote you a number.

sections.title: Why Alaska interests are harder to value than most
sections.html:
Most royalty buyers who focus on Texas, Oklahoma, and Louisiana simply won't touch an Alaska interest, because the comparable sales data that makes pricing fast in the Permian or Haynesville doesn't exist up there in the same volume. Fewer transactions means we can't just pull three recent nearby deals and price off them the way we would in Reeves County. Instead we go straight to production data filed with the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Comreview and build a decline model specific to your well or unit.

That extra work is exactly why we're careful not to throw out a number before we've actually looked at your interest. If someone offers you a fast, generic quote on an Alaska royalty without asking which field, which unit, and what your decimal interest is, be skeptical — it likely means they're guessing, not pricing.

sections.title: ANCSA land, state leases, and what you actually own
sections.html:
Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act corporations hold enormous mineral estates that don't trade like typical private minerals, and if your family's interest connects to a Native corporation share, that's a different legal animal from a fee mineral interest you'd inherit in the Lower 48 — usually not something we or anyone else can simply buy outright. What we do buy is privately held royalty and override interests carved out of leases on state or federal acreage, which is a more limited but real category of ownership.

If you're not sure which bucket your family's paperwork falls into, send us what you have. We'll tell you plainly whether it's something we can make an offer on or something that needs to stay exactly as it is, rather than stringing you along toward a deal that was never going to close.

sections.title: The realities of North Slope production and pricing
sections.html:
North Slope crude has historically priced against Alaska North Slope (ANS) benchmark, which trades close to global Brent pricing rather than the WTI number most of the country watches, and that spread has moved around a lot over the years depending on shipping costs and global demand. Anyone valuing your interest should be working off ANS realizations, not a generic WTI assumption — using the wrong benchmark alone can throw an offer off meaningfully.

Legacy North Slope fields like Prudhoe Bay have been producing since the late 1970s and are well into decline, while newer developments on the western Slope have added fresh volumes in recent years. Where your specific interest sits in that mix, old and declining versus newer and still building, changes the shape of the value conversation, and we'll walk you through which one applies to you.

sections.title: How we work with Alaska owners from a distance
sections.html:
Almost none of our Alaska sellers live in Alaska, and neither do we — these interests get passed down to heirs scattered across the Lower 48 who inherited a royalty statement with no context attached to it. Everything can be done by mail, phone, and email; we don't need you to travel, and we don't ask you to sign anything before you've had a chance to review it and, if you'd like, run it past your own attorney.

We'll pull the title and production history ourselves once you send us your decimal interest, unit or lease name, and a recent statement. From there we build an offer, walk you through exactly how we got to that number, and close through a title company or escrow attorney once you're ready. There's no cost to get a number, and no obligation if it's not the right time to sell.

faqs.q: Do you buy royalty interests tied to Alaska Native corporation land?
faqs.a: Generally we buy privately held royalty and overriding royalty interests carved from leases on state or federal acreage, not shares in an ANCSA corporation itself. Send us your paperwork and we'll tell you clearly which category your interest falls into.

faqs.q: Is North Slope crude priced the same as Texas oil?
faqs.a: No. Alaska North Slope crude trades against its own ANS benchmark, which tracks closer to global Brent pricing than the WTI price most of the Lower 48 watches, and that spread varies with shipping and global demand.

faqs.q: You inherited a small Alaska royalty and have no idea what field it's in. Can you help you figure that out?
faqs.a: Yes. Send us whatever paperwork or statements you have, even incomplete ones, and we'll research the unit, lease, and production history before we ever discuss a number.

faqs.q: Why do so few companies buy Alaska mineral interests?
faqs.a: Alaska has far fewer private mineral transactions than Texas, Oklahoma, or Louisiana, so pricing data is thin and each interest typically requires individual research rather than a quick comparable-sales lookup. Many buyers simply skip the state because of that extra work.

faqs.q: Do you need to travel to Alaska to sell your interest?
faqs.a: No. We handle Alaska interests entirely by phone, mail, and email, and closings run through a title company or escrow attorney, the same as any other state we work in.

items.name: Inherited Mineral Rights
items.meta: Inherited a royalty check or a deed with no context? Here's how to figure out what you have, what it's worth, and whether keeping it makes sense.

sections.html:
The first sign is usually a small check in the mail with a well name you've never heard of, addressed to a parent who's no longer around to explain it.

We hear some version of this story every week. A parent or grandparent passes, and somewhere in the estate paperwork is a mineral deed, or a royalty statement, or just a line in the will mentioning 'mineral interests in Section 14' with no further explanation. Nobody in the family has ever driven past the land, doesn't know which county it's actually in half the time, and has no idea whether it's worth calling a lawyer over or just letting it sit.

Our own family went through this exact thing two generations back, minerals that had been in the ground since before anyone alive remembered signing a lease. There's no shame in not knowing what you've got. Mineral ownership is one of the few assets in America that regularly gets passed down without anyone explaining how it works, and the paperwork that comes with it is genuinely confusing even to people who deal with it professionally.

sections.title: Figuring Out What You Actually Inherited
sections.html:
Start with whatever documents exist: a deed, a division order, a recent royalty check stub, or the probate inventory itself. Any of these should show a county and state, sometimes a specific well or unit name, and often a fraction representing your ownership share. If you have nothing but a check, the operator's name printed on it is your starting point — a call to their owner relations line will usually confirm what interest is on file and where it sits.

It's worth knowing there's a real difference between owning the mineral rights themselves and owning a royalty interest carved out of someone else's minerals. If you inherited the underlying minerals, you may also have decision rights over future leasing. If you inherited a royalty interest specifically, you're entitled to a share of production income but don't control leasing decisions. The deed language tells you which one you have, and it changes both what you're allowed to do with it and roughly what it's worth.

sections.title: Producing, Leased, or Sitting Quiet
sections.html:
An interest that's already producing and paying royalties is the easiest to evaluate, since there's real payment history to look at. An interest that's leased but not yet drilled has value tied to the bonus that was paid and the operator's plans for the acreage, which can be harder to pin down. And an interest with no lease and no production at all still has value if it sits in an active play, based on what's happening on neighboring tracts, but that value is more speculative and we say so plainly rather than inflating a number to make an offer look better.

Multiple heirs inheriting the same interest is extremely common, and it doesn't have to be resolved before you get information. We can work with one heir gathering facts on behalf of siblings, or with several heirs at once, and nothing has to be signed until everyone who needs to agree actually agrees.

sections.title: The Keep-or-Sell Decision
sections.html:
There's no universally right answer here, and we'll tell you that even though we're in the business of buying. Some families keep an inherited interest for decades, collecting whatever royalty comes in and passing it to the next generation the same way it was passed to them, which works fine as long as everyone stays organized about division orders and address changes. Other families decide the ongoing administration, the unpredictable income, or simply having six heirs try to agree on every future decision isn't worth it, and selling converts an uncertain future income stream into a known amount today.

A decline curve matters here more than people expect. Most producing wells pay their highest royalties in the first few years, then taper off as the well ages, sometimes gradually and sometimes fast depending on the formation. An interest that's paying well today may pay a fraction of that in five years, which is one honest reason some heirs choose to sell into a strong payment history rather than watch it shrink.

sections.title: How the Sale Actually Works if You Choose It
sections.html:
If you decide to sell, we start with the same documents you'd gather anyway — deed, division order, recent statements — confirm the interest against county and operator records, and put a written offer in front of you with no pressure to accept it. If probate is still open, we can work alongside your executor and attorney and time the transfer to whatever the estate's process requires; you don't need probate fully closed before getting a number, only before the deed can actually transfer.

For interests split among several heirs, we can buy everyone's share in one transaction if the family agrees, or buy from individual heirs separately if some want to sell and others want to keep their portion. Either way the title work has to be clean before anything closes, and we'll flag early if there's a probate gap or missing heir that needs to be resolved with your attorney first.

faqs.q: You do not have any paperwork, just a check. Where do you start?
faqs.a: Call the operator's name printed on the check or statement and ask for their owner relations department. They can confirm what interest is on file, which well or unit it's tied to, and often send you a copy of the division order.

faqs.q: Do all the heirs have to agree before we can sell?
faqs.a: Only for the actual sale. We can talk with one heir, gather facts, and give a preliminary number well before everyone has signed off, so the family has real information to discuss before making a decision together.

faqs.q: Is it better to sell now or wait and see if the well keeps producing?
faqs.a: Most producing wells decline over time, often paying their best royalties in the first several years. There's no single right answer, but some heirs prefer selling into a known payment history rather than betting on where the decline curve lands years out.

faqs.q: What if probate isn't finished yet?
faqs.a: We can still give you a written offer and work alongside your executor and attorney on timing. The deed simply can't transfer until the estate's process allows it, which your attorney will guide.

faqs.q: Does inheriting mineral rights create a tax bill by itself?
faqs.a: Inheriting alone typically doesn't trigger income tax, but ongoing royalty checks are taxable income, and a later sale has its own tax treatment. Talk to your CPA about your specific basis and situation before deciding.

items.name: Got an Unsolicited Offer?
items.meta: A stranger's letter offering to buy your royalty interest arrived out of nowhere. Here's how to check whether the number is fair before you respond.

sections.html:
A letter shows up referencing a well you may or may not know about, offering to buy something you didn't know was for sale.

This happens more than people expect. A company you've never heard of gets your name and address from county deed records or an operator's division order list, and mails an offer to buy your mineral or royalty interest, sometimes for a specific dollar amount, sometimes just inviting you to call for a quote. It can feel intrusive, and it raises an obvious question: is this a fair number, or are they hoping you'll sign without checking?

We get asked to review these letters constantly, and the honest answer is it varies. Some unsolicited offers are reasonable. Others are priced well under what the interest is actually worth, betting that most owners won't take the time to verify before signing. There's no way to know which kind you're holding without doing a little homework first, and we're glad to help with that even if you never sell to us.

sections.title: Why You're Getting These Letters
sections.html:
Mineral ownership records are public. County deed and probate records, along with operator division orders, are searchable, and a number of companies build their entire business around mailing offers to owners of record across active plays, sometimes targeting counties where recent well permits or completions suggest values are rising. Getting a letter doesn't mean anything unusual is happening with your specific interest — it usually just means you're on a list compiled from public records, the same list anyone, including us, could compile.

It's also common to get several of these letters over time from different buyers, sometimes with noticeably different offer amounts for what should be the same interest. That spread by itself is a useful signal — if buyers can't agree within a reasonable range, it's worth taking the time to understand why before you sign anything back.

sections.title: How to Check Whether an Offer Is Fair
sections.html:
Start with your most recent royalty statements, if you have any. A rough industry rule of thumb multiplies a healthy year of royalty income by a range tied to the well's expected remaining life and current activity nearby — but that's only a starting sanity check, not a precise formula, since actual value depends heavily on the specific well's decline curve, remaining reserves, and what's happening in the surrounding unit. If an unsolicited offer comes in far below what that rough math suggests, it's worth questioning before you respond.

It also helps to ask the letter's sender directly how they calculated their number. A legitimate buyer should be able to explain their reasoning — production history, decline assumptions, comparable regional activity — rather than just stating a figure and asking for a signature. If they're vague or evasive about how they got there, treat that as a signal to get a second opinion before moving forward.

sections.title: Getting a Second Opinion Costs You Nothing
sections.html:
Send us the same information you'd send any buyer — your deed or division order, recent statements if you have them, and the letter you received if you're comfortable sharing it — and we'll give you our own written number based on the same production and activity data. You're under no obligation to sell to us, and there's no cost to compare. Plenty of owners use our number purely as a benchmark to negotiate with the original buyer, or simply to confirm the offer they already have in hand was fair.

We'd rather you take the time to compare than sign the first letter that lands in your mailbox, even when that means we don't end up buying the interest ourselves. A fair market has multiple buyers checking each other's numbers, and you're allowed to make them compete for your interest.

sections.title: Red Flags Worth Watching For
sections.html:
Be cautious of letters that pressure a fast response, use language implying the offer expires in days, or discourage you from seeking a second opinion. A genuine buyer isn't threatened by you taking time to verify, and urgency tactics are a common way to keep an owner from discovering a low offer was actually below market. Also double-check that the legal description and decimal interest referenced in the letter actually match what you own — mismatches happen, sometimes innocently, sometimes not.

If you ever feel unsure about a letter's legitimacy at all — a company you can't find any record of, contact information that doesn't check out, or a deed they're asking you to sign that looks unusual — it's worth having an attorney review it before you sign anything, regardless of who the buyer is.

faqs.q: How did this company get your name and address?
faqs.a: Most likely from public county deed, probate, or division order records, which anyone can search. Receiving a letter doesn't mean anything unusual is happening with your interest specifically.

faqs.q: Is the offer you received a fair price?
faqs.a: It depends on the interest's actual production history and the well's remaining life, which the letter alone won't tell you. Send us the same details and we'll give you a written comparison number at no cost.

faqs.q: Should you be worried if the offer seems really low?
faqs.a: It's worth questioning, not panicking over. Some unsolicited offers are priced well under market value on the assumption owners won't verify. Ask the sender to explain their math, and get a second opinion before responding either way.

faqs.q: Do you charge anything to review an offer you already have?
faqs.a: No. Comparing an existing offer against our own written number costs nothing and comes with no obligation to sell to us.

faqs.q: The letter says the offer expires in a few days. Should you rush?
faqs.a: A legitimate buyer generally isn't hurt by you taking a reasonable amount of time to verify the number. Manufactured urgency is one of the more common signs an offer may not hold up under a second look.

items.name: Fractional & Small Interests
items.meta: A 1/64th royalty check for $11 a month isn't worth the tax paperwork to some owners. Here's why small fractional interests exist and how to sell one.

sections.html:
Somewhere on your grandfather's land patent, one section got left to four kids, then to their kids, and now your check is a fraction of a fraction.

The family experience behind Royalty Buyer followed this same path before the desk reviewed another owner's sale. A great-grandfather held a full quarter section. By the next generations, that interest had passed among six heirs and their children, and the royalty statement carried a decimal with four zeros in front of it. The check that came with it some months barely covered the stamp to mail the statement.

That's just how mineral ownership works over three or four generations. Nobody did anything wrong — land that once passed to one heir now splits among a dozen, and each of those splits gets divided again by whatever fraction the original deed or will specified. A lot of owners in that position never learn what their interest is actually called or how it compares to a neighbor's, they just see a small number on a check and assume that's simply what mineral rights are worth.

sections.title: How an Interest Gets This Small
sections.html:
Start with a single owner holding an undivided mineral interest under 160 acres. Pass it to four children in equal shares and each now holds 1/4. Each of their estates splits among three grandchildren and each grandchild holds 1/12. Extend that two more generations, through remarriages, wills that split unevenly, and the occasional heir who sold off their piece separately along the way, and it's common to find interests measured in tiny fractions — 1/128th, 1/256th, sometimes further out than that.

None of this makes the interest illegitimate or worthless, it just means the royalty check on any given well gets divided by that same fraction before it reaches you. If a well produces $4,000 a month in gross royalty across all owners and your net mineral acreage works out to 1/256th of the unit, your share of that check is a very small number, even though the well itself is producing perfectly well.

sections.title: Why Small Interests Are Genuinely Hard to Manage
sections.html:
Operators are legally required to pay every owner of record, no matter how small the share, but many states let them hold payments below a minimum threshold — often $25 or $100 — in suspense until enough accumulates to cut a check, or until the owner requests it directly. That means some heirs go years without seeing a dollar even though the interest is actively producing, simply because their share never crosses the payout floor in any single period.

There's also a real administrative cost that falls on you, not the operator. Every 1099 from a producing interest, however small, is income you have to report. Every operator merger or unit reconfiguration means a new division order to sign. Every time you move, you have to update your address with every operator across every well your family's interest touches, and if a fractional owner dies without updating their own address, that piece can slip into unclaimed property or an unresolved probate that nobody in the family even remembers exists.

sections.title: What a Small Interest Is Actually Worth
sections.html:
Value on a fractional interest isn't calculated any differently than a full interest — it's still based on production history, remaining reserves, and current activity in the unit — but the total dollar figure scales down with the fraction, the same way the royalty check does. A tiny interest under an active, high-volume well can still be worth a real number, while a tiny interest under a marginal stripper well may not clear much at all. We look at your actual decimal interest and the well's real production before we say anything about value, rather than guessing off the size of the fraction alone.

What we hear most from owners in this position isn't really about the dollar amount, it's about wanting to be done carrying a piece of paperwork that pays less than it costs in time to track. Consolidating several small fractional interests into one payment, or simply cashing one out entirely, is a legitimate reason to sell even when the number itself is modest.

sections.title: Selling a Small Interest Without the Runaround
sections.html:
Because small fractional interests are common and the file work is largely the same regardless of size, we don't treat a tiny interest as a lesser transaction. We'll pull the well's production and payment history, confirm your decimal interest against the operator's division order, and put a written offer in front of you — often within days, since there's usually less title history to untangle on a long-held family interest than on one that's changed hands recently.

If you own several small fractional pieces scattered across different wells or even different counties, inherited from different branches of the family over the years, we can look at all of them together and give you one combined picture instead of forcing you to sort out each interest on your own before you even know if it's worth the effort.

faqs.q: Is a fractional interest like 1/128th even worth selling?
